title: Tax residency of companies — s 6(1) ITAA 1936
summary: Australian tax residency of a company is determined by three alternative limbs in the s 6(1) ITAA 1936 definition of 'resident': (1) incorporated in Australia; (2) carries on business in Australia AND has central management and control in Australia (Koitaki Para Rubber Estates Ltd v FCT (1941) 64 CLR 241; Harding v FCT [2019] FCAFC 29); or (3) voting power controlled by Australian-resident shareholders. Passing ANY one limb makes the company a resident. The Part X Australian resident carve-out (CFC context) and DTA tie-breakers (place of effective management) are boundary nodes. Subsection coverage: s 6(1) 'resident' company limbs all mapped; s 995-1 ITAA 1997 cross-reference; individual and trust residency are separate maps.

nodes.label: Determine whether the company is a resident under s 6(1) ITAA 1936
nodes.body: Corporate tax residency is determined by the s 6(1) ITAA 1936 definition of 'resident' for companies: a company is a resident if it is incorporated in Australia; or if it is not incorporated in Australia, it carries on business in Australia and has either its central management and control (CM&C) in Australia or its voting power controlled by shareholders who are Australian residents.

nodes.label: Is the company incorporated in Australia?
nodes.body: Incorporation in Australia (under Australian law) makes the company a resident regardless of where it is managed or carries on business. This is the first and simplest limb of the corporate resident definition.

nodes.label: Is the company's central management and control in Australia?
nodes.body: Central management and control (CM&C) is the highest level of control — where the company's strategic decisions are made and where the directors actually exercise their powers, not where day-to-day operations occur. Koitaki Para Rubber Estates Ltd v FCT (1941) 64 CLR 241: company incorporated in Papua was held a resident because its directors met and controlled the company from Sydney.

cases.title: Koitaki Para Rubber Estates Ltd v Federal Commissioner of Taxation

nodes.label: Is the voting power of the company controlled by shareholders who are Australian residents (applicable only where the company carries on business in Australia)?
nodes.body: The third limb under s 6(1)(b): a company that is not incorporated in Australia but carries on business in Australia is a resident if its voting power is controlled by shareholders who are Australian residents. This limb only applies after the carries-on-business precondition is satisfied. If the company does not carry on business in Australia, the voting-power test is not reached and the company is non-resident regardless of who controls its voting power.

nodes.label: RESIDENT COMPANY — taxed on worldwide income
nodes.body: A resident company is taxed on worldwide income (s 6-5 ITAA 1997) at the corporate rate, with access to the participation exemption (Subdiv 768-A dividends, 768-G gains) and franking.

nodes.label: FOREIGN RESIDENT COMPANY — taxed only on Australian-source income
nodes.body: A foreign resident company is taxed only on Australian-source income: dividends, interest, royalties, and gains on taxable Australian property (Div 855). CFC rules (Part X ITAA 1936) may attribute the income of controlled foreign companies to Australian shareholders.

nodes.label: BOUNDARY — Is the company a 'Part X Australian resident' for CFC purposes?
nodes.body: Under Part X ITAA 1936 (CFC rules), a company that is a Part X Australian resident cannot itself be a CFC. Sections 332(2)(a) and 333(2)(a) each require that the company NOT be a Part X Australian resident. A company that becomes a Part X Australian resident displaces the CFC analysis entirely — this is a threshold carve-out, not a continuity test.

nodes.label: INTERACTION — s 995-1 ITAA 1997: 'Australian resident' cross-reference
nodes.body: Section 995-1 of ITAA 1997 defines 'Australian resident' as 'a person who is a resident of Australia for the purposes of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936'. The s 6(1) definition therefore applies for all purposes of the 1997 Act, including Div 855 (foreign residents' CGT) and the participation exemptions.

nodes.label: DTA TIE-BREAKER — Is the company a dual resident under the applicable DTA?
nodes.body: If the company is a resident under Australian domestic law AND also a resident of a treaty partner country under that country's domestic law, the applicable double tax agreement (DTA) tie-breaker resolves the dual residency. The tie-breaker typically looks to the company's place of effective management (POEM). This only applies to companies that are Australian residents under the domestic s 6(1) test.

nodes.label: Corporate residency determination complete — apply the applicable tax treatment
Does the company carry on business in Australia?
nodes.body: Under s 6(1)(b) ITAA 1936, a company that is not incorporated in Australia must carry on business in Australia before either the CM&C test or the voting-power test can make it a resident. If the company does not carry on business in Australia, it is a foreign resident regardless of where its management or shareholders are located.
